RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the Housing Authority:

  1. Approve the Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale’s 2024-2025 Annual Report
  per Health and Safety Code Section 34328 and 34328.1; and,
  2. Authorize the Executive Director or their designee to submit the report to the State
  of California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).

BACKGROUND

The Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale (Housing Authority) was activated by the
City Council on April 9, 1997, pursuant to California Housing Authorities Law. In
accordance with Health and Safety Code Sections 34328 and 34328.1, the Housing
Authority must prepare a complete report of its activities during the previous fiscal year
by October 1. The annual report must be filed with the City Clerk and submitted to the
California Department of HCD. As part of the reporting process, the Housing Authority
may recommend legislation or other actions necessary to carry on housing and
community development programs in the State of California.

DISCUSSION

Staff has prepared a report describing the Housing Authority’s affordable housing
activities utilizing the Housing Authority assets, the Low- and Moderate-Income Housing
Funds assumed from the Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale
(former Redevelopment Agency), and the Housing Asset Funds proceeds from the

  I.  PREFACE

  In accordance with California Health and Safety Code Sections 34328 and
  34328.1, a Housing Authority is required to file an annual report at least once a
  year with the clerk of the respective city or county and with the Department of
  Housing and Community Development (HCD) describing its activities for the
  preceding year. The report shall contain information adequate for the city, county,
  or department to determine that the requirements of Section 34312.3 have been
  met for any activity undertaken pursuant to that section.

II.  REPORT OF AFFORDABLE HOUSING ACTIVITIES

  a. Assumption of Housing Assets from Former Redevelopment Agency
  The Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale (Housing Authority) assumed the
  housing assets and obligations of the Low- and Moderate-Income Housing Fund
  (LMIHF) of the former Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale
  (former Redevelopment Agency) in January 2012, effective February 1, 2012,
  pursuant to Assembly Bill No. 26 (2011-2012 1st Ex. Sess.). The proceeds from
  the assets assumed from the former Redevelopment Agency are held in the
  Housing Authority’s Low- and Moderate-Income Housing Asset Fund (HAF).

  b. Management of Housing Authority-Owned Properties
  The Housing Authority owns and operates the three Mobile Home Parks (Boulders
  at the Lake, Boulders at the Ranch I, and Boulders at the Ranch II). Newport Pacific
  Capital Company, Inc. manages the properties. The percentage of units required
  by Health and Safety Code Section 34312.3(c) to be occupied by specified income
  levels was met. The Housing Authority will continue to monitor the properties to
  confirm continued compliance.
  The Housing Authority owns and operates 291 units of affordable rental housing
  (Impressions, La Quinta, Park Vista, and Summerwood Apartments). Newport
  Pacific Capital Company, Inc. manages the properties. The percentage of units
  required by Health and Safety Code Section 34312.3(c) to be occupied by
  specified income levels was met, and the Housing Authority will continue to monitor
  the properties to confirm continued compliance.
  The Housing Authority has no tenancy terminations or Section 8 voucher
  terminations associated with victims of domestic violence to report.

Page 2  Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale

   Multi-family Mortgage Revenue Bonds were issued by the former Redevelopment
  Agency in 1998 for the acquisition and rehabilitation of the Mobile Home Parks and
  were refinanced in 2003 and 2005. The Promissory Note for the bonds to the
  former Redevelopment Agency was assumed by the Housing Authority in 2003,
  when the title was transferred from the prior owner, and is paid from net cash flow
  generated by the three mobile home parks. The Housing Authority is current in its
  payment obligations.
  Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds were issued in 2015 to acquire and rehab 291
  units of affordable rental housing (the Impressions, La Quinta, Park Vista, and
  Summerwood Apartments). The Housing Authority's Promissory Note for the
  bonds is paid from the net cash flow generated by the four apartment properties.
  The Housing Authority is current in its payment obligations.

III.  OTHER REQUIRED INFORMATION
  The Housing Authority, in its capacity as the housing successor to the former
  Redevelopment Agency, is also required to conduct an independent financial audit
  for the previous fiscal year and to prepare a report on its housing activities as
  specified in Health and Safety Code Section 34176.1(f). The audit, report, and the
  Housing Authority budget will be presented to the Housing Authority Board under
  separate cover.
  The Housing Authority recommends legislation to address the State of California
  Department of Finance’s refusal to use Redevelopment Property Tax Trust Funds
  (RPTTF) to pay Housing Authority administrative costs relating to the transferred
  housing assets and obligations of former Redevelopment Agencies.

  In addition, the Housing Authority recommends legislation to address the impacts
  of “Accessory Dwelling Units” by right (SB1069) on sewer infrastructure, traffic, and
  parking in residential zones, as an unfunded mandate.

Staff recommend that the City Council:

BACKGROUND

Pursuant to Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the City
Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly reports on investments to the City
Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The reports shall detail the
type of investment, issuer’s name, purchase date, maturity date, amount of deposit, and
interest rate. This information shall be provided for all City and Successor Agency pooled
investments and for Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds,
Assessment Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts managed by outside
Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the City and Successor Agency’s
investment activity. They provide information on assets, allocations, average maturities,
yields, and book valuations. The interest rates presented are the most current rates
available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.

DISCUSSION

Compliance with Investment Policy

For July, the City’s invested portfolio totaled $315,916,723, a decrease of $5,366,230
from the previous month and a decrease of $17,467,848 compared to the prior year.
The monthly decrease was due to the maturity of Government Agency Paper and a
withdrawal from the Local Agency Investment Fund to the general fund to cover
operational costs.

The par value of the Successor Agency’s portfolio as of July was $12,113,285. The
balance increased by $47,688 from the prior month due to interest earned during the
month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, US Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies: 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and,
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to meet the
City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the City invests in two
pooled funds, the Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and the California Asset
Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily operational activities and
can be used during economic uncertainties for ongoing operating and maintenance
needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City and Successor
Agency meet cash flow requirements.

The City’s LAIF balance at the end of July was $106,623,145, a decrease of $3,782,073
due to a withdrawal in the current month.

The Successor Agency’s LAIF balance at the end of July was $3,942,545, an increase
of $42,726 from the prior month, due to interest earned.

The City’s CAMP balance at the end of July was $53,145,462 compared to $52,947,078,
in June. The increase is due to interest earned.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-054, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale to transfer unclaimed checks from their respective funds to the
  general fund pursuant to California Government Code Section 50050-50057.

BACKGROUND

Section No. 50050-50057 of the California Government Code states that “Except as
otherwise provided by law, money, excluding restitution to victims, that is not the
property of a local agency that remains unclaimed in its treasury or in the official custody
of its officers for three years is the property of the local agency after notice if not claimed
or if no verified complaint is filed and served. At any time after the expiration of the three-
year period, the treasurer of the local agency may cause a notice to be published once
a week for two successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation published in the
local agency. At the expiration of the three-year period, money representing restitution
collected on behalf of victims shall be deposited into the Restitution Fund or used by the
local agency for purposes of victim services

DISCUSSION

The City Treasurer desires to follow the guidelines set by California Government Code
Section 50053. Section No. 50053, which states, “When any such money becomes the
property of a local agency and is in a special fund, the legislative body may transfer it to

year period ending June 30, 2025, is $5,502.06.

One vendor came forward and requested a replacement check within the forty-five-day

FISCAL IMPACT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-065, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale authorizing the execution and delivery of a Custody Agreement
  regarding funds of the City of Palmdale Community Facilities District No. 93-1
  (Ritter Ranch) and approving related actions.

BACKGROUND

In connection with the proposed master planned development of an area known as Ritter
Ranch (Project), the City formed City of Palmdale Community Facilities District 93-1
(CFD 93-1) to finance certain public facilities for the Project. The City issued Special Tax
Bonds for CFD 93-1 in 1995 (93-1 Bonds) to finance the facilities (Facilities).

The property in CFD 93-1 and the 93-1 Bonds were purchased in 2020 by Preston
Hollow Capital, LLC (PHC), who later transferred the land to RdR Development
Holdings, LLC (RdR), a limited liability company for which PHC is the sole member.
Collectively, PHC and RdR are referred to below as the RdR Parties.

DISCUSSION

In September 2022, the RdR Parties were prepared to proceed with development of the
first phase of the Project, expected to include up to 1,180 residential units (Phase 1).
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council
Re: Adopt Reso. No. CC 2025-065
September 2, 2025
Page 2

They requested, and the City formed, a new community facilities district for the Phase 1
property portion of the Project (CFD 2022-3) to fund public infrastructure and
improvements necessary for the development of the Project. The RdR parties expect to
cancel all the outstanding CFD 93-1 Bonds prior to proceeding with the issuance of
special tax bonds for CFD 2022-3.

There are approximately $2.7 million in proceeds of the 93-1 Bonds restricted for use
on the Facilities. The expenditure of these funds is governed by an Acquisition
Agreement, dated February 1, 1995, as Amended and supplemented by the Supplement
No. 1. to Acquisition Agreement ( No. A-4262), dated as of November 1, 2016 (together,
the Acquisition Agreement) which provided for the use of bond proceeds for the Facilities
and by a Phase 1 Interim Agreement – Ritter Ranch Development (No. A-7796) (Interim
Agreement), dated April 20, 2022, for the purpose of allocation existing proceeds of 93-
1 Bonds to complete certain of the Facilities as designated in the Acquisition Agreement.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-067, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale recognizing the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department for its
  commitment to transparency and community trust, and expressing support for
  State Legislation promoting identification and accountability in law enforcement.

BACKGROUND

On July 11, 2025, the federal court issued a preliminary injunction against federal
enforcement agencies, including ICE, prohibiting the detention of individuals based on
one, or a combination of the following factors: 1. Race/ethnicity; 2. Speaking Spanish or
speaking English with an accent; 3. Presence at a particular location (e.g. bus stop, car
wash, tow yard, day laborer pick up site, agricultural site, etc.); and 4. The type of work
one does.

In response to this ruling, the LASD amended its operational processes to include specific
procedures to identify federal agents by on-scene LASD officers, including direction to
request identification or agency credentials and record the encounter on the officer’s
body-worn camera.

On or about July 29, 2025, County intervened in the federal suit, and the Los Angeles
County Board of Supervisors directed County Counsel to draft an ordinance prohibiting

On August 19, 2025, the City Council directed staff to prepare a resolution expressing
support for the actions taken by County and LASD in response to federal immigration

DISCUSSION

The City contracts with LASD for police services and there is no confirmed federal

The City Council requested a resolution expressing support and recognizing the actions
taken by the County and LASD to confirm the identity and legitimacy of individuals acting

RECOGNIZING THE LOS ANGELES COUNTY SHERIFF’S DEPARTMENT
FOR ITS COMMITMENT TO TRANSPARENCY AND COMMUNITY TRUST,
 AND EXPRESSING SUPPORT FOR STATE LEGISLATION PROMOTING
  IDENTIFICATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN LAW ENFORCEMENT

  WHEREAS, the City of Palmdale is proudly served by the Los Angeles
County Sheriff’s Department (LASD), whose deputies demonstrate
professionalism, courage, and dedication in protecting the safety of Palmdale
residents; and

  WHEREAS, the City recognizes that enforcement activities, including those
that intersect with federal agencies such as U.S. Immigration and Customs
Enforcement (ICE), can create heightened tensions, fear, and confusion within
the community; and

  WHEREAS, community trust and officer safety are best maintained when
deputies are clearly identifiable during enforcement operations, and when the
use of facial coverings is limited to situations where they are operationally or
medically necessary; and

  WHEREAS, these protocols have strengthened trust and communication
between law enforcement and the community, particularly during complex and
sensitive operations; and

  WHEREAS, these best practices provide reassurance to residents, reduce
confusion during enforcement activities, and reinforce the City’s commitment
to transparency and accountability in public safety; and

  WHEREAS, legislation currently before the California State Legislature
seeks to extend these same standards of identification and accountability
statewide, aligning with the leadership and example already demonstrated by
LASD in Palmdale and across Los Angeles County.
 Resolution No. CC 2025-067
Page 2 of 2

  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale as follows:

  1.  The City of Palmdale expresses its support for LASD deputies as
  they navigate the challenges of federal enforcement actions within
  the community, and reaffirms the City’s commitment to fostering
  collaboration and mutual respect between law enforcement and
  residents.

  2.  The City of Palmdale supports pending state legislation aimed at
  enhancing transparency and accountability in law enforcement
  statewide.

  3.  The City Clerk shall transmit copies of this resolution to the Los
  Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, the Los Angeles County Board
  of Supervisors, and the City’s state legislative delegation to
  communicate the City’s appreciation and support.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve the First Amendment to Agreement No. A-9221 with RSG, Inc., for
  consultant services related to the Home Rehabilitation and Accessibility Programs,
  increasing the Agreement by $69,610 for a not to exceed total of $150,000 for a
  three-year term with option for two additional years; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to execute the Agreement
  No. A-9221 with RSG, Inc., including minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City Council approved the five-year plan (The Plan) for the State of California
Department of Housing and Community Development’s (HCD) Permanent Local
Housing Allocation (PLHA) Program on July 14, 2020. The PLHA funding is generated
from the Building Homes and Jobs Act, SB2, which established a $75 recording fee on
real estate documents to increase the supply of affordable housing in California. The
Plan includes activities for home rehabilitation and home accessibility for owner-
occupied single-family residences. The City Council approved the Home Rehabilitation
and Accessibility programs on March 20, 2024.
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council

DISCUSSION

RSG, Inc. (RSG) has provided the City assistance with program administration for the
Home Rehabilitation and Accessibility Programs, including program design, participant
selection, loan and grant documentation, inspections, contractor bid documentation,
construction management, and case management, which includes annual compliance
monitoring. Original PLHA program administration funding of $80,390 is estimated to
assist at least 20 participants with repairs needed. With the additional funding of
$69,610, through PLHA years 2021 and 2022, RSG, Inc. will be able to process an
additional 25 participants with repairs and accessibility. The current agreement with
RSG has two years remaining and an option for two additional years. Funding for PLHA
year five will be allocated for additional case management when received from the
Department of Housing and Community Development.

$69,610; funds are budgeted and available in FY 2025-26 in account 24164007-782965.

Administration of the Single-Family Home Rehabilitation and Home Accessibility

The Home Accessibility Program provides housing rehabilitation loans up to $30,000

improvements, including, but not limited to, installing ramps, ADA door hardware, and

owner-occupied single-family homes. It concentrates on health and safety emergency
repairs, such as leaking roofs, broken plumbing, inoperable water heaters, and
inoperable heating and cooling units.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend the City Council:

Approve the deaccession of the Back Home sculpture at the Palmdale Transportation
Center (PTC) in accordance with the Public Art Commission’s Deaccession of Artwork
Policy and Chapter 15.01 of the Palmdale Municipal Code.

BACKGROUND

In 2014, the sculpture “Back Home” by Sol Mesz was installed at the PTC. The artist
crafted the sculpture from repurposed materials, adorned with recycled glass leaves.
The artist fused glass components, while the City’s Maintenance staff constructed the
branches using repurposed materials. Notably, this project was completed prior to the
adoption of the Public Art Master Plan and Municipal Public Art Guidelines.

DISCUSSION

The materials selected by the artist did not withstand the harsh Antelope Valley climate.
Over time, the components have failed, causing the piece to deteriorate. In 2018, a welder
was hired to restore the piece and extend its longevity, with the artist’s approval.
Unfortunately, the piece has continued to decline, no longer representing the artist’s
original intention. Considering the materials used and the environmental conditions it was
exposed to for over a decade, the lifespan of this sculpture has reached its end.
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council
Re: Deaccession of Back Home Sculpture
September 2, 2025
Page 2

Staff reached out to the artist, who has declined to claim the sculpture. Considering the
following criteria specified in the Deaccession of Artwork Policy, staff recommend
proceeding with the deaccession of this piece:

    The condition or security of the artwork cannot be reasonably guaranteed;
    The artwork requires excessive maintenance or has faults of design, materials, or
  workmanship, and repair or remedy is impractical or unfeasible;
    The artwork has been damaged or has deteriorated, and repair or remedy is
  impractical or unfeasible; and,
    The artwork’s physical or structural condition poses a threat to public safety.
    Alteration or disassembly of the original artwork prohibited under the Visual Artists
  Rights Act (VARA).

The Public Art Commission reviewed this item on March 25, 2025, and recommend
the deaccession of the Back Home Sculpture for City Council approval in accordance
with Chapter 15.01 of the Palmdale Municipal Code.

Additionally, a new sculpture for the roundabout at the PTC was approved as part of
the Five-Year Public Art Work Plan, aiming to enhance the overall aesthetic of this
regional transportation hub.

FISCAL IMPACT

$1,000; for the removal and disposal of the Back Home sculpture. Funds are budgeted
and available in FY 2025-26 in the Public Art Contract Services account.

  DEACCESSION OF ARTWORK POLICY

PURPOSE

The Public Art Program maintains the City of Palmdale’s collection of artwork for the
benefit of Palmdale citizens. Removing an artwork from the collection (deaccessioning)
is a delicate matter and must be managed according to strict guidelines, outlined below.
When necessary, the Public Art Program, with the input of the Public Art Commission, will
incorporate into this policy additional guidelines. No work may be deaccessioned until
the appropriate guidelines set forth below have been observed.

POLICY

  1. Any proposal for removal, destruction, or relocation of an artwork will be submitted
  to the Public Art Coordinator and reviewed by the Public Art Commission according
  to the policies and procedures contained herein and will be deliberate and
  independent of political pressures, fluctuations in artistic taste, popularity, and
  public opinion.

  2. Deaccession will be undertaken only after issues such as artist’s rights, public
  benefit, censorship, copyrights, and legal obligations have been carefully
  considered. The final decision with respect to deaccession of artworks owned by
  the City will rest with the Public Art Coordinator upon approval by the Public Art
  Commission.

  3. As needed, the City’s artwork collection will be evaluated by the Public Art
  Coordinator and reported to the Public Art Commission to determine the condition
  of each artwork and determine whether there is artwork that should be
  deaccessioned.

DEFINITIONS

ARTISTS: Individuals recognized by critics and peers as professional practitioners of the
visual arts based on the quality of their body of work, educational background and
experience, past public commissions, sale of works, exhibition record, publications, and
production of artwork.

  1
 ARTWORK: Works created uniquely by an artist and as defined in Chapter 15.01.040 of
the Palmdale Municipal Code.

DEACCESSION: The procedure for the removal of an artwork owned by the City and the
determination of its future dispensation.

DEACCESSION NOTIFICATION: A written letter to the artist or donor referencing the
applicable condition(s) of the artwork and describing reasons why the deaccession review
needs to be undertaken.

GUIDELINES

It is important for the City of Palmdale to retain the right to remove any artwork on City-
owned land and in City-owned facilities. Any artwork owned by the City may be eligible
for deaccession with the exception of an artwork that is accompanied by verified legal
stipulations that the artwork may not be deaccessioned. During the review process, the
artwork will remain accessible to the public in its existing location unless it poses a threat
to public safety.

Artwork may be reviewed for deaccession at any time at the initiative of the Public Art
Coordinator or Public Art Commission members. Review also may be initiated by the
artist regarding the artwork she/he created, by an artist’s designated heir(s), or by legally
recognized representative(s).

Artwork may be considered for review for deaccession if one or more of the following
criteria apply:

  1. The condition or security of the artwork cannot be reasonably guaranteed.

  2. The artwork requires excessive maintenance or has faults of design, materials or
  workmanship and repair, or remedy is impractical or unfeasible.

  3. The artwork has been damaged or has deteriorated and repair or remedy is
  impractical or unfeasible.

  4. The artwork’s physical or structural condition poses a threat to public safety.

  5. The artwork is proved to be inauthentic or in violation of existing copyright laws.

  6. The artwork is not, or is only rarely, on display because the City lacks a location
  for its display.

  7. No suitable site is available for relocation or exhibition, or significant changes in
  the use, character or design of the site have occurred which affect the integrity of
  the artwork.

  8. Changes to the site have significantly limited or prevented the public’s access to
  the artwork.

  2
   9. The site where the artwork is located is undergoing privatization.

  10. Deaccession is requested by the artist.

  11. If there are more that six works (excluding editions of prints) by the same artist in
  the City-owned portable collection, or more than three permanently installed works
  on public display in the City-owned collection or in private development, the Public
  Art Coordinator may recommend to the Palmdale Public Art Commission that the
  City retain only a representative selection of the artist’s work.

  12. If the artwork has been lost, stolen, or is missing, the Public Art Commission may
  approve formally deaccessioning it from the collection while retaining a record in
  the collection database showing that the artwork has been deaccessioned.

PROCEDURES

Deaccession will begin with a formal Deaccession Request letter which can be initiated
by the Public Art Commission, the Public Art Coordinator, the artist, or the artist’s
designated heirs or legally appointed representative. The Deaccession Request will be
submitted to the Public Art Coordinator and will describe the applicable condition(s)
outlined in the Guidelines above, and the reasons why the deaccession review needs to
be undertaken. A Deaccession Request must also contain information about the
requestor’s relationship to the artwork and stake in deaccessioning the artwork.

Deaccession Requests will be reviewed by the Public Art Coordinator who will make every
reasonable effort to contact the artist who created the artwork named in the Deaccession
Request and any other known parties with a vested interest in the artwork. When
permanently sited artworks are proposed for deaccession, the Public Art Commission will
convene at a regularly scheduled meeting to discuss the reasons deaccessioning is being
considered, and to gather comments on the deaccession proposal. The Public Art
Coordinator will present a deaccession recommendation to the Public Art Commission,
which may decide to convene an ad hoc committee comprised of practicing conservators,
art appraisers, registrars, and/or other visual arts professionals to review and advise the
Public Art Commission on the Deaccession Request. In presenting the Deaccession
Request, the Public Art Coordinator will provide the necessary information to the Public
Art Commission, from, but not limited to, the following list:

  1. Artist’s name, biographical information, samples of past artwork, and resume.

  2. A written description and images of the artwork

  3. Artist’s statement about the artwork named in the Deaccession Request.

  4. A description of the selection/acquisition process and related costs that was
  implemented at the time the artwork was selected.

  5. A formal appraisal of the artwork provided by a qualified art appraiser.

  3
   6. Information about the origin, derivation, history, and past ownership of the artwork.

  7. A warranty of originality of the artwork.

  8. Information about the condition of the artwork and the estimate cost of its
  conservation provided by a qualified visual arts conservator

  9. Information about the images of the artwork’s site.

  10. For permanently sited artwork: Information about how community feedback about
  the artwork was collected and the outcome of that feedback.

  11. Feedback from the Director of the City department responsible for operating and
  maintaining the artwork site.

  12. A detailed budget of all aspects of conservation, maintenance, repair, installation,
  operation, insurance, storage, and City staff support.

  13. The artist’s contract with donor or comparable legally binding document with Proof
  of Title.

  14. Deed of gift restrictions, if any.

DEACCESSION REVIEW CRITERIA

  A. In addition to the condition and security of the artwork as stated above, the review
  criteria for Deaccession Requests includes, as appropriate:

  1. ARTISTIC EXCELLENCE: Qualifications and professional reputation of the
  artist; craftsmanship, conceptual content, style, form.

  2. VALUE OF ARTWORK as determined by a professional appraiser.

  3. RELATIONSHIP TO EXISTING COLLECTION OF ARTWORKS: Style,
  form, scale, diversity, quantity, quality, longevity, and compatibility with the
  existing collection of artwork and goals of the Public Art Program.

  4. AVAILABILITY OF CITY SUPPORT: The availability of necessary funding
  for conservation, maintenance, and/or repair; exhibition and storage space;
  real property for siting artwork; and City staff support.

  5. RELATIONSHIP TO SITE: Accessibility, public safety, and social, cultural,
  historical, ecological, physical, and functional context of the artwork in
  relation to the site, both existing and planned.

  6. LEGAL CONSIDERATIONS: Issues related to liability, insurance, copyright,
  warranties, ownership, theft, vandalism, loss, indemnification, and public
  safety. The City Attorney shall review the recommendation of the Public Art
  Program and the Public Art Commission to determine whether there are any

  4
   legal restrictions that would prevent deaccessioning the object. The City
  Attorney’s approval must be obtained.

  7. TIMING: Safety or hazard emergencies, relevant construction schedules,
  and the allowance of sufficient time for a normal review process.

  8. ACQUISITION PROCESS: Method by which the artwork was acquired and
  accessioned into the collection of artworks (i.e., donation, loan,
  commission).

  9. COMMUNITY FEEDBACK: Community feedback about the artwork, its site,
  and its condition solicited via a publicly noticed meeting or placed on the
  agenda of the Palmdale Public Art Commission.

  10. RESTRICTIONS: Any recognized restrictions associated with the artwork.

  B. Members of the Public Art Commission may request to view the actual artwork
  during the Deaccession Review process.

  C. The Public Art Commission will make a recommendation to City Council, with or
  without conditions, or reject the Deaccession Request based on the review criteria
  described in this policy. City Council makes final decisions on Public Art
  Commission recommendations regarding deaccession of artwork

REMOVAL PROCESS

The deaccessioned artwork will be removed from the collection of artworks through
methods administered by the Public Art Program. In all cases, the artist or the artist’s
designated heir(s), or legally recognized representative(s) will be given, when possible
and within a reasonable time frame, the opportunity to purchase the artwork for the fair
market value (as determined by a qualified art appraiser), or, if the artwork is determined
to be of negligible value, the artist will be given the opportunity to claim the artwork at the
artist’s own cost.

  A. When the artist does not purchase or claim the deaccessioned artwork, the
  methods which may be utilized to remove artwork through public negotiations
  include but are not limited to:

  1. Sale. Proceeds from the sale will be deposited into the Public Art Fund.
  Written acknowledgement by Finance to place revenues from the sale of
  deaccessioned artwork into the Public Art Fund, must be obtained. Legal
  public notice regarding the sale will be published in local newspapers.

  i.  The artist/donor will be given the right of first refusal to reacquire the
  work at fair market value, original price, or nominal value, depending
  on the recommendation of the Public Art Commission. The cost of
  removal of the artwork may be reflected in the amount set.

  ii.  Sell the work through a dealer.

  5
   iii.  Sell the work through sealed bidding or public auction.

  2. Trade or exchange of a deaccessioned artwork for another by the same
  artist.

  3. Donation of deaccessioned artwork to a non-profit organization, institution,
  or agency.

  4. Destruction. This method shall only be used in the following instances:

  i.  The entire artwork has been damaged or has deteriorated and repair
  or remedy is impractical or unfeasible.

  ii.  Most of the artwork has been damaged or has deteriorated and
  repair or remedy is impractical or unfeasible, and any remaining
  intact parts of the artwork are deemed to have negligible value, and
  the artist is not willing to claim the remaining parts at the artist’s own
  cost.

  iii.  Public safety can be protected only by destroying the artwork.

  iv.  Every effort to locate the artist, kin or donor has failed.

B. When possible, the method for removing the artwork from the collection of artworks
  will be selected to ensure that the highest reasonable price is received. Any profits
  received by the City through the sale, trade, or auction of a deaccessioned artwork
  will be deposited into the Public Art Fund administered by the Public Art Program.

C. In keeping with the California Resale Royalties Act, Civic Code Section 986, if a
  deaccessioned work is sold or exchanged, 5% of the sale price or exchange value
  of any work over $1,000 will be given to the artist who created the work, provided
  that the artist can be located by reasonable means. If the artist cannot be found,
  the Resale Royalties shall be transferred to the California State Arts Council, a
  state agency.

D. The Public Art Coordinator will remove acquisition numbers and labels from the
  artwork and coordinate its physical removal from the City’s collection.

E. The Public Art Coordinator will report on the sale or exchange of artwork at the
  next regularly scheduled meeting of the Public Art Commission, following receipt
  of all funds or the completion of the sale, exchange, or donation.

F. The Public Art Coordinator will transmit a report informing the City Council of the
  removal of the artwork from the City’s collection.

G. The Public Art Coordinator will maintain a Deaccession File that includes individual
  folders on each deaccessioned artwork. These files will include all documentation
  regarding the artwork.

  6
   H. Artworks may not be sold, traded, or donated to current employees of the City of
  Palmdale, their business partners, or their immediate family members. Current
  elected officials, Palmdale Public Art Commission members, their business
  partners, and their immediate family members may not buy, receive, or own any
  artwork which has been deaccessioned from the collection of artworks.

Nothing in these guidelines will limit the City’s ability to take appropriate action to protect
public health and safety in the event of an emergency.

BACKGROUND

BrightLife Designs, LLC, a premier provider of commercial lighting and holiday décor,
specializes in creating custom holiday light displays, delivering tailor-made designs,
professional installation, removal, and complete turnkey services, including storage.

In 2024, a Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued to secure a holiday light and
decoration vendor, leading to the selection of BrightLife Designs, LLC. A one-year
contract was executed, with an option to extend it to two additional one-year terms.

DISCUSSION

City staff are pleased with the quality and professionalism demonstrated by BrightLife
Designs, LLC, in providing holiday lighting and décor for Poncitlán Square during the
2024 holiday season. Their work received positive community feedback, attracting
thousands of visitors from Thanksgiving through New Year’s. BrightLife Designs
incorporated City-owned decorations into the display and worked closely with City
maintenance staff to ensure proper power distribution to each installation.

In 2025, BrightLife Designs will expand the holiday display to include décor around the
Civic Center and an enhanced presentation within Poncitlán Square. The Parks and
Recreation Department will further activate the space with seasonal programming such
as a movie night, live music, and pictures with Santa, complementing the expanded
display. In addition, as part of America’s Semiquincentennial (250th) anniversary on July
4, 2026, BrightLife Designs will install a patriotic display in Poncitlán Square, anticipated
to be one of the City’s primary attractions for this historic celebration.

BACKGROUND

EPIC is required to submit this staff report and related meeting minutes to the California
Energy Commission (CEC) per Power Source Disclosure Program regulations to
demonstrate compliance. For the 2024 reporting cycle, CEC staff will generate the
Power Content Labels (PCLs) on behalf of retail suppliers, including EPIC. CEC staff
aim to provide the 2024 PCLs to retail suppliers by mid-September 2025. The
requirement for retail suppliers to provide the PCL to the CEC by October 1, 2025, will
be considered fulfilled without additional action. EPIC will be required to display the 2024
PCL on its website by October 1, 2025, and provide written promotional materials to its
customers by December 31, 2025.

To fulfill its Power Source Disclosure Program reporting obligations for 2024, EPIC, as
a public agency, must provide the CEC with the City Council’s attestation regarding the
accuracy of information included in the annual Power Source Disclosure Report.

DISCUSSION

California Public Utilities Code requires all retail sellers of electric energy, including
EPIC, to disclose “accurate, reliable, and simple-to-understand information on sources

of energy” that are delivered to their respective customers via an annual PCL. The PCL
is analogous to a nutrition label, conveying information regarding the various power
sources/products that are procured on behalf of each retail electricity customer. Each of
California’s retail electricity sellers, including EPIC, will have unique PCLs based on
internally adopted procurement policies, statutory procurement mandates, and related
power purchases that were completed during the reporting year.

The PCL format is highly prescriptive, offering little flexibility to retail sellers when
presenting such information to customers. The CEC administers these requirements
under California’s Power Source Disclosure Program. Information presented in each
PCL includes the proportionate share of total energy supply related to specific fuel
sources/resource categories, including both renewable and conventional generating
technologies.

An emission factor for each retail service offering, as calculated using the CEC’s
prescribed methodology, is also provided in the PCL. If a retail seller procures a certain
percentage of its energy requirements from the market at large (meaning, sources of
power that cannot be traced back to a specific generator), the PCL must identify such
purchases as “unspecified sources of power.” It is common for most retail electricity
sellers to utilize “unspecified power.”

In accordance with statewide mandates and internally adopted planning targets, EPIC
procured a substantial portion of its electric energy supply from generating resources
utilizing various renewable fuel sources in 2024. Renewable fuel sources may include
biomass & waste, hydroelectricity, solar, geothermal and wind.

For EPIC Power customers, please note that 47% of total energy supply was sourced
from RPS-eligible (CEC certified) renewable energy resources in 2024. For EPIC Power
100, 100% of the energy delivered was sourced from renewable energy resources.

While developing EPIC’s data for the 2024 PCL, CalChoice and its technical consultants
performed a detailed review of all power purchases completed for the 2024 calendar
year. The review performed by CalChoice and its technical consultants found no
inaccuracies or inconsistencies in such information, which was subsequently entered in
EPIC’s annual Power Source Disclosure report.

To fulfill its attestation requirements for 2024, Council is being asked to provide an
attestation covering EPIC’s Annual Report.

Consistent with applicable regulations, all customers currently enrolled in the EPIC
program will receive the 2024 PCL via electronic communication or U.S. mail on or
before December 31, 2025. Additionally, the 2024 PCL will be displayed on the EPIC
website by October 1, 2025.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Award and Approve Agreement No. A-9317 with Applied Research Associates
  Inc., for PN 922, Citywide Sign Inventory and Retroreflectivity Assessment Project
  (Project), for a total not to exceed amount of $418,979, which includes a contract
  amount of $380,890, plus a 10% contingency amount of $38,089;

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to execute Agreement No.
  A-9317 with Applied Research Associates Inc., including minimal and/or non-
  substantial changes; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to approve amendments to
  the contract for additional or changed scope of work up to the 10% contingency
  amount approved by the City Council.

BACKGROUND

The City took over the maintenance of all traffic signs from the Los Angeles County
Department of Public Works in 2000. Since then, the City has maintained all signs using
in-house staff. However, the City has never carried out a complete inventory or
assessment of traffic signs.

In 2005, the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) mandated that municipalities
perform a study of sign retroreflectivity and must have an implementation and
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council

management strategy designed to maintain regulatory and warning sign retroreflectivity
at or above the minimal levels set by the FHWA in the Manual of Uniform Traffic Control
Devices (MUTCD).

City staff attempted to perform this study with in-house staff; however, due to past
staffing level reductions and budgetary constraints over the years, they could not
complete the survey. Currently, the City has approximately 20,400 traffic signs within its
jurisdiction, which would be subject to the survey.

DISCUSSION

On May 2, 2005, the City released a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for the Project,
via PlanetBids. On June 4, 2025, the City received three (3) bids for the project, which
have been reviewed and are summarized below:

 Bidder  Location
 Applied Research Associates Inc.  Ventura, CA
 National Data & Surveying Services  Los Angeles, CA
 Precision Material Management  Cerritos, CA

Applied Research Associates, Inc. (ARA) was selected as the most qualified proposal
based on its demonstrated experience and technical capabilities. ARA previously
worked with the City on projects, such as the Pavement Inventory and Condition Study,
delivering them on time and within budget. In addition, ARA has video inventory of the
street network and will be extracting the sign assets for the inventory. Once complete
they will deploy teams for the retroreflectivity testing requirement, providing efficiencies
in both time and cost.

This Project includes a comprehensive field survey to identify and catalog all regulatory,
warning, guide, and object marker signs as defined in the MUTCD and to ensure that
the City meets the mandated retroreflectivity requirements. Each sign will be geo-
tagged, rated by condition, and uploaded into the City’s Lucity Asset Management
System. This contract will take 180 days to complete.

$418,890; Sufficient funds are budgeted in Capital Improvement, Local Transportation
Fund Article 8.

Task I – Sign Inventory
Conduct a comprehensive field survey to identify and catalog all regulatory, warning,
guide, and object marker signs as defined by CAMUTCD

Exclude signs that are mounted in private streets, mounted on wood 4x4 posts
(Caltrans or County-maintained), or pertaining to exclusive use by bikes/pedestrians,
walking/hitchhiking, Adopt-A-Highway, and those with blue or brown backgrounds

Geo-tag each sign's location (±3') using high-accuracy GPS coordinates
Photograph each sign for documentation and verification purposes
Document each sign with the following comprehensive attributes:
Designation number and classification in accordance with the MUTCD. If the sign is
not a MUTCD sign, use “N-STD” as the sign code.
Word description of sign (e.g., 35 mph speed limit sign, pedestrian crossing
warning sign, flashing beacons). Include unique sign information, such as “No

Task II – Field Retroreflectivity Assessment
Perform retroreflectivity assessment of all signs in the field using a retroreflectometer
that complies with ASTM E1709, Standard Test Method for Measurement of Signs
Using a Portable Retroreflectometer

Process includes:
1. Testing both legend and background reflectivity values
2. Assigning a status of “Acceptable” or “Unacceptable” based on current CAMUTCD
minimums
3. Using calibrated signs for each CAMUTCD color combination, maintained near
minimum thresholds, and verified prior to each field session
4. Excluding retroreflectivity testing for:
“No parking, stopping, or standing” signs
Non-CAMUTCD signs or other non-traffic control signage
All measurements will be tied to GIS records and included in final reporting.

BACKGROUND

DryTown Water Park, originally opened in 2006, added a four-lane mat racer slide in
2012, and is ready for its next major attraction.

On June 3, 2025, City Council approved an agreement with WhiteWater West Industries,
Ltd. (WhiteWater) to design, manufacture, and install the new attraction featuring a 35-
foot-tall tower and three integrated water slides: the Pool Sider, AquaTube, and Freefall.

The ride will be built on the north side of the park, in a grassy area, and aims to expand
operations and boost visitor appeal. The design-build project by Bergman includes:

    Structural foundations;
    A new mechanical building and pump systems; and,
    Walkways, drainage, landscaping, lighting, and irrigation.

These improvements will be integrated with the park’s current infrastructure where
possible. Bergman and WhiteWater plan to have the new attraction ready for the 2026
season.

DISCUSSION

Design-Build Contractor

On June 25, 2025, the Project was advertised for design-build bids through the Planet
Bids electronic platform. Four (4) vendors registered as prime contractors. By the bid
deadline on July 25, 2025, the City received one (1) electronic bid, which is summarized
below:

confirmed it has the necessary construction and design experience to complete the
Project. Its recent work includes projects for Wild Rivers Water Park (Irvine), Sea World
(San Diego), and the County of San Bernardino, along with other projects in Florida,
South Carolina, and Texas. They met all bid requirements.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

BACKGROUND

As an entitlement and participating jurisdiction, the City of Palmdale receives an annual
allocation of funds from HUD under its Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and
Home Investment Partnership (HOME) Programs. Additionally, the City received a special
allocation of Community Development Block Grant COVID-19 (CDBG-CV) funds, as
authorized by the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act enacted
on March 27, 2020, to be used exclusively on eligible activities that prepare for, prevent,
and respond to the COVID-19 pandemic. As an entitlement and participating jurisdiction,
the City is required to prepare and obtain HUD approval of a Consolidated Plan covering
a period of five years. The 2020 Five-year Consolidated Plan was approved by Council
and submitted to HUD in June 2020. The plan addresses various HUD-required issues,

Progress the jurisdiction has made in carrying out its strategic plan and its action plan.

This 2024-2025 Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) is the City of
Palmdale’s report to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) describing
the use of federal Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME Investment
Partnerships Program (HOME) funds during the fifth program year of the 2020-2024 Consolidated
Plan period, covering July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025. This CAPER will also describe the use of the
Community Development Block Grant Coronavirus (CDBG-CV) funds, as authorized by the
Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act, enacted on March 27, 2020, and
programmed into the City’s 2019-2020 Annual Action Plan, as amended.

The City receives CDBG and HOME funds from HUD on a formula basis each year and receives a
special allocation of CDBG-CV funds. In turn, the City implements projects and awards grants and
loans to nonprofit, for-profit and public organizations for projects in furtherance of the adopted
Consolidated Plan. The CDBG and HOME programs provide a wide range of eligible activities for
the benefit of low and moderate-income Palmdale residents. The CDBG-CV funds provide eligible
activities that prepare for, respond to, and prevent COVID-19 pandemic.

For the 2024-2025 program year, the City received $1,500,651 of CDBG funds $4,000 of CDBG
Program Income and has $970,881 of unprogrammed prior year funds and $526,111 of HOME
funds and has $1,539,385 of unprogrammed prior year funds from HUD. Together, with prior
year(s) funding available, a total of $4,541,028 was allocated to projects in the 2024-2025 Action
Plan. This investment of CDBG and HOME funds was a catalyst for positive change in the
community. Together with other federal, state, and local investments, HUD resources allowed
the City and its partners to:

  •  Provide fair housing services for 225 residents
  •  Provide homelessness prevention and assistance services to 10,787 residents
  •  Provided tenant-based rental assistance to 25 senior households
  •  Provide for ADA improvements at Q-12 that will benefit 2,070 residents when complete

Additionally, the City continued eligible activities for the special allocation of CDBG (CDBG-CV) in
the amount of $1,932,895 to be used exclusively on eligible activities that prepare for, respond
to, and prevent the COVID-19 pandemic. The CDBG-CV funds were programmed in the 2019-
2020 Action Plan:

  •  Respond to COVID-19 pandemic by providing emergency rental assistance to 7

During the program year, the City and its housing and community development partners made
progress on several 2024-2025 activities as well as some multi-year activities that continued
during the program year. All CDBG and HOME funded activities addressed specific high priority
objectives identified in the 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan. All CDBG-CV funded activities prepared
for, responded to, or prevented the COVID-19 pandemic.

The CDBG-funded South Antelope Valley Emergency Services (SAVES) activity provided much-
needed services through the CDBG entitlement funding and expanded their services with CDBG-
CV funding. On March 4, 2020, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health issued a State
of Emergency and ordered all non-essential businesses to close due to the COVID-19 Pandemic.
On March 16, 2020, SAVES adopted the COVID-19 National Emergency model to become an
emergency-only food distribution center. SAVES re-designed from client choice to a no-contact
drive-thru. SAVES also coordinated with local churches and community group volunteers to
deliver emergency food to shut-in senior residents. The Federal Government’s public health
emergency declaration expired May 11, 2023, the State of California’s declaration expired
February 28, 2023, and Los Angeles County’s declaration expired March 31, 2023. The City of
Palmdale continues to serve residents affected by the pandemic. As a result, SAVES served people
within all residential tracts of the City, meeting the Low and Moderate Clientele National
Objective. During the program year, 10,787 food orders were distributed to needy households.

Most CDBG funds were allocated to public facilities and infrastructure improvement activities to
benefit low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, provide disabled access, provide facilities for
homelessness prevention services, or directly support affordable housing during the program
year. The project scope for the ADA Improvements at Q-12 was increased to include street
improvements. Construction is anticipated to be completed by August 2025. Funds have been
allocated for the construction and improvement of sidewalk, curb, and gutter infrastructure
along 3rd Street East to enhance pedestrian safety and neighborhood accessibility, estimated to
be completed in December 2025.

The 2024 HOME-funded Tenant Based Rental Assistance (TBRA) assisted 25 unduplicated
extremely low-income senior households (age 62 or older) experiencing a severe housing cost
burden (more than 50% of household income goes to rent).

To address housing and community development needs in Palmdale, the City leverages its CDBG
and HOME entitlement grants with a variety of funding resources in order to maximize the
effectiveness of available funds. The primary funding sources for leveraging CDBG and HOME
funds in Palmdale are Housing Successor Agency housing asset funds, redevelopment Successor
Agency funds and the Redevelopment Property Tax Trust Fund (RPTTF) funds.

During the program year, the Juniper Grove project located at the southeast corner of Division
and East Ave R in Palmdale leverages HOME funds of $728,678 and CDBG funds of $250,000
with Low Income Housing Tax Credits through the California Tax Credit Allocation Committee,
yielding $22,310,650 of Tax Credit Equity, which was under construction. Additional financing of
$33,211,811 was secured from other sources, including multiple grants from the Los Angeles
Community Development Authority. This project provides for the new construction of 101 units
of housing serving families with rents affordable to households earning 30-50 percent of the
area median income (AMI).

Additional CDBG leveraging opportunities were available for SAVES. The organization received
more than $10,000 in monetary donations from the community, along with in-kind food
contributions from local businesses and the Palmdale School District, valued at over $3 million.

HUD requires HOME Participating Jurisdictions (PJs) to match 25 percent of their HOME annual
allocation. In accordance with 24 CFR 92.222, PJs satisfying the distress criteria established by
the HOME Program regulations are provided a match reduction. Match reductions are granted
due to fiscal distress, severe fiscal distress, and Presidential disaster declarations. For the 2024-
2025 program year, the City of Palmdale received a 50 percent match reduction from HUD.

The Juniper Grove Affordable Housing Project financing closed in October 2020. The City
committed $728,678 of HOME funds and $250,000 of CDBG funds for site assemblance. The

50 units are designated for individuals experiencing homelessness, and 2 units are for managers.
The project has been completed, and the certificate of Occupancy was issued February 2024,
with the overall project being completed June 2025. TBRA, the City supported 25 Senior
households through ongoing rental assistance (PR-23 records 25 households, as reported in
tables 2, 11, and 12).

In future annual action plans, the City anticipates continuing to invest HOME funds to address
housing affordability for renters and homeowners through the creation of new units,
rehabilitation of existing substandard units, and the provision of TBRA to the City’s most
vulnerable residents – extremely low-income senior citizens experiencing a severe housing cost
burden.

The City is actively seeking a certified Community Housing Development Organization (CHDO)
with capacity to develop housing to increase the likelihood of meeting the HOME program
requirement that 15 percent of each allocation be committed to a CHDO project within 24
months. The active TBRA Program will ensure that HOME funds are effectively committed on
time to meet HUD’s 24-month commitment deadline. As a result of these actions, the City will be
able to strategically invest the remaining HOME funds in affordable housing development or
rehabilitation projects at a point in time when these projects are shovel ready with all other
financing commitments in place.

In Los Angeles County, the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) is the lead agency
coordinating the Continuum of Care (CoC). LAHSA is a joint powers authority for the City and
County of Los Angeles (with the exception of the Cities of Long Beach, Pasadena, and Glendale).
A ten-member Commission governs LAHSA. Each of the County’s five Supervisors appoints one
(1) commissioner while the Mayor and City Council of Los Angeles appoint another five (5)
members. LAHSA plans, coordinates, and manages resources for the County’s homeless
programs. In addition, LAHSA provides technical assistance, data, and other planning resources
to many of the incorporated cities within the County, including the City of Palmdale. LAHSA
develops and oversees a comprehensive strategy to address homelessness.
Additionally, in February, 2016, the Los Angeles Board of Supervisors approved
an unprecedented action plan of nearly two dozen interlocking strategies, focusing on six key
areas to combat homelessness. The City of Palmdale has been one of over 100 community
groups, cities and county leaders who continue to actively participate in the planning and
implementation of these strategies to address homelessness. As part of the County strategy, the
City of Palmdale participated in a process to create a City-specific plan to prevent and combat
homelessness. In addition to participating in County-wide stakeholder meetings and as a member
of the (CoC), the City of Palmdale participates in a regional approach to address homelessness
within the Antelope Valley Service Planning Area No. 1 (SPA 1). SPA 1 covers approximately 2,500
square miles of desert and forest, from the Kern County line on the north, to the San Bernardino
County line on the east, the Ventura County line on the west and the Angeles Forest on the south.
The homeless count conducted by LAHSA in January 2020 estimated that the number of homeless
persons in SPA 1 increased forty-four percent to 4,755. This count indicated that the number of
homeless in Palmdale had decreased by 9 percent to 289 people homeless persons in 2020. In
February 2025, the number of persons in SPA 1 was 6,753 and 198 encountered in Palmdale.
The City participates in the Antelope Valley Homeless Coalition, an inter-agency council with
approximately 50 participants. Through this participation, the City is able to coordinate efforts
and resources with local homeless service providers including Los Angeles County’s Coordinated

The City of Palmdale Housing Authority was formed in 1994 under the State of California Housing

overall increase of 112 percent from 1990 to 2020, LACDA has made changes to address the need
for the growing senior population. In August of 2013, HUD approved LACDA’s application to
designate 13 public housing senior developments as housing for elderly families only (62 years
or older).

Actions taken to encourage public housing residents to become more involved in management
and participate in homeownership

LACDA actively encourages residents to be involved in the organization through resident councils
and active participation in housing authority decisions via surveys and other forms of
engagement. LACDA also maintains quarterly newsletters for Section 8 tenants, public housing
residents, and Section 8 property owners.

LACDA encourages residents to explore homeownership opportunities. LACDA currently
administers the Family Self-Sufficiency (FSS) program for public conventional housing and
Housing Choice Voucher program residents. The FSS program provides critical tools and
supportive services to foster a resident’s transition from financial and housing assistance to
economic and housing self-sufficiency, most importantly homeownership.

To support this effort, LACDA utilizes marketing materials to outreach and further promote the
program’s requirements and benefits to all public housing residents. For families that are eligible
to participate, a Contract of Participation (COP) is prepared to govern the terms and conditions
of their participation, and an Individual Training Service Plan (ITSP) is created that outlines the
following: supportive services to be provided, activities to be completed by the participant, and
agreed upon completion dates for the services and activities. The COP is valid for five years and
may be extended to allow the family to meet their ITSP goals.

Once the COP is established and the family experiences an increase in tenant rent as a result of
earned income, an escrow account in their name is established and increased earned income is
deposited into this account. Escrow accounts are disbursed to the family once the family has

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Open a Public Hearing to receive public comments on the PLHA Formula 5-Year
  Plan Amendment for years 2020-2025;

  2. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-064, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale authorizing the application and amending the PLHA Formula 5-Year
  Plan with the State of California Department of Housing and Community
  Development (HCD) PLHA Program, and;

  3. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to take all actions convenient
  and necessary to submit and execute the amendment, and all related documents,
  including making necessary non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

In 2017, the Building Homes and Jobs Act, SB2, established a $75 recording fee on real
estate documents to increase the supply of affordable housing in California. The PLHA
Program was established for these funds. Of the funds collected, seventy percent (70%)
is allocated to local governments and administered locally for affordable housing. Of these
funds, ninety percent (90%) are allocated to the local governments based on the HUD
CDBG federal fiscal year 2017 allocation process. The City has been allocated an
estimated $4,674,384 over the five-year plan period. The PLHA guidelines require not

more than five percent (5%) of the funds to be used for Administration, twenty percent
(20%) of the funds to be expended for Affordable Owner-Occupied Workforce Housing
and prioritize investments that increase the supply of housing to households that are at
or below sixty percent (60%) of the area median income.

The City’s PLHA Five-Year Plan includes programs for down payment assistance for
households who are low- and moderate-income, rehabilitation of owner-occupied
residences, accessibility modifications in lower-income owner-occupied housing, and
assistance for persons experiencing or at risk of homelessness. The PLHA Five-Year
Plan estimates funding for the preservation and ownership assistance of 70 units of
housing.

DISCUSSION

The City proposes to amend the percentage allocation of PLHA funding between
programs within the 5-year Plan period to increase its program for affordable rental
housing and increase funding for its down payment assistance program. The homeless
services allocation has been reduced and, due to the changes in funding sources, is
being redirected from the Navigation Center concept.

FISCAL IMPACT

$573,510; An additional appropriation of $573,510 will align the total budget with the
PLHA allocation amount, which was only an estimate at the time of adoption.
Administrative adjustments between program lines may be required to remain consistent
with program guidelines. Year 5 funds will be brought forward for appropriation once the
allocation amount is confirmed by HCD.

The City of Palmdale plans to use PLHA funds for the following eligible activities: 1) Rehabilitation or preservation of owner-occupied housing for extremely low to low-income households (primarily senior and disabled individuals); 2. Provide a construction loan for the

The City will prioritize investments that increase the supply of housing for households with income at or below 60% AMI through the following: 1. Construction of new rental housing projects that will include units with affordability for low income households at or below 60% of
area median income.

RECOMMENDATION

Appointment of two Councilmembers to form an Ad Hoc Subcommittee to review and
provide recommendation for a possible partnership with PWD for the Littlerock Dam
Recreation Project.

DISCUSSION

On August 19, 2025, the City Council requested the formation of an ad hoc subcommittee
consisting of two councilmembers to review and provide direction as to the best course
of action for the City in possibly partnering with the PWD for the Littlerock Dam recreation
project.

The Palmdale Water District has created its own subcommittee to assess its
recommendation. The two subcommittees may meet to confer and recommend the best
course of action.
